## Review of last class

- Communication is a process of exchanging information and creating shared meaning through encoding and decoding messages
- Engineers must consider their audience's background and knowledge level when communicating
- Professional communication has time constraints and deliverables with firm due dates

## Email fundamentals and importance

- Email is the primary form of written business communication in professional settings
- Professionals spend ~2.5 hours per day checking and writing emails
- Emails serve multiple critical functions:
  - Exchange information
  - Demonstrate professionalism and competence
  - Create legal records of decisions, requests, and procedures
  - Coordinate work approval and tracking
- Appropriate uses: routine messages, task-oriented content, fact-based information, non-sensitive topics
- Inappropriate for personal or sensitive matters (use secure portals instead)
- Always double-check reply vs. reply-all to ensure correct recipients

## Email structure and formatting

All professional emails follow the same basic structure:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Subject line"] --> B["Greeting & name"]
    B --> C["State main point immediately"]
    C --> D["Body: supporting details"]
    D --> E["Action item/call to action"]
    E --> F["Professional closing"]
    F --> G["Signature block"]
```

- **Subject line:** Precise, concise summary (e.g.,

); enables filing and quick identification
- **Greeting:** Use proper titles (Dr., Professor, Mr./Ms.) unless explicitly given permission to use first names; avoid assumptions
- **Opening:** Lead with the main point immediately—do not bury the lead
- **Body:** Use bold headers, bullet points, or numbered lists for clarity; include only necessary details
- **Closing:** Summarize, state required action, and end courteously
- **Signature block:** At minimum include name and email; can add title, department, phone, and professional note; set as default in email account

## Tone, timing, and netiquette

- Emails are formal communication—avoid casual language
- **Timing matters:** Sending emails outside business hours (e.g., 3–4 a.m.) can signal false urgency or disrespect; schedule emails to arrive during business hours
- **Response expectations:** Reply within 1–2 business days; if taking longer, acknowledge receipt and set expectation
- **Follow-ups:** Acceptable to check in after stated deadline; consider setting calendar reminders
- **Priority flags:** Use sparingly;

is context-dependent and can backfire if overused
- **Recipients:** Only include those who need to know; CC for informational copies, BCC for mailing lists or confidential distribution
- **Composition safety:** Write email first, add recipient email address last to prevent accidental sends; assume any email may be forwarded to supervisors, clients, or legal review

## Addressing challenges and managing emotions

- **Neutrality effect:** Recipients may perceive positive messages as emotionally neutral in writing
- **Negativity bias:** Neutral messages may be decoded as negative due to lack of nonverbal cues
- **Cyber incivility:** Can manifest as disrespect (active), passive-aggressiveness, or silence; avoid flaming or delayed responses
- **De-escalation strategies:**
  - Show respect and consideration in all communication
  - When receiving a charged email, step back and take time before responding
  - Focus on the task content, not emotional reaction
  - Respond professionally regardless of tone received

## Practical formatting example

Compare ineffective vs. effective emails:

**Ineffective:**
- Subject: "Update"
- Body: Large text block, unclear main point, buried key information

**Effective:**
- Subject: "Project Alpha—2 day delay Phase 2 testing platform"
- Opens with main problem and context
- Uses headers and bullet points for readability
- Closes with action items and path forward

## Key takeaways for professional emails

- Subject line must summarize content concisely
- State your main point in the opening (first 1–2 sentences)
- Use formatting (bold, bullets, numbers) to aid scanning
- Maintain professional, appropriate tone throughout
- Use names and greetings to foster morale and respect
- Ensure email is easy to read—assume recipient is busy
- Remember: your email is a reflection of your professional competence
